anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L1 mine has a 5x5x3 isometric world, four diamonds, click-ray occlusion, view rotation, a visible lava/support hazard, and limited extraction durability. Fluke L1 has only two required individuals among three 2D bodies and no rotation or scale variation, but still needs a moving-lens hit and two remembered species; current Fluke L4 adds six required identities, three decoys, full pose variation, and repeated self-ordering. Thus Fluke is materially above this anchor on identity memory while lacking the mine's 3D occlusion and physical-collapse control.

evidence.explanation: The approved baseline is L1/simplified and its active L1 parameters are four targets, one lava block, one support and no sealed targets.
The generator implements isometric projection and frontmost ray visibility, rather than a static flat selection.
Success requires all diamonds removed without collapse and with nonnegative durability.
Fluke creates individual notch identities, moving layouts and required IDs for the listed species.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L2 constellation requires moving the cursor until one field converges into a visible shape, then making one final click within a radius; decoy basins and animated noise affect the probe but there is no multi-item census or post-click dependent state. Fluke L1 is a small multi-photo version with two listed individuals, and Fluke L4 requires six identity decisions over ten layouts, so the assigned baseline is clearly above this one-click anchor in memory and repeated state-dependent observation.

evidence.explanation: The approved configuration is L2/full with one convergent target field and a single click-based interaction.
The visible constellation response is a cursor-conditioned field with target and decoy progress.
The grader checks one click's distance to the expected point, not a sequence of changing board decisions.
Fluke replays each shutter against the current epoch and requires the complete set of required identities.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L3 board couples continuous tilt to momentum, wall and well collisions, three ordered lamps, and a final cup; a bad trajectory can require recovery. Fluke L4 has stronger individual-identity and no-mark memory than that board, but its action is a direct lens placement plus shutter and has no route, momentum or collision planning. The cross-mechanic burden is different, so L4 is plausible for Fluke's memory/perception axis without claiming it dominates the approved L3 physical-control task.

evidence.explanation: The approved baseline is L3/full with three lamps, three walls/wells and active physics parameters.
The board visibly advances physical motion each tick and accepts held analog input or simplified compass input.
The grader replays acceleration, friction, speed, collision and hazard physics.
Fluke instead uses moving polygon poses and a magnified identity card for each direct inspection.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L4 courier traverses an 18x11 course through five face-locked barriers while die orientation is hidden except at sparse scanners; every move changes future gate legality. Fluke L4 requires six distinct identity choices across reshuffled scenes and exact moving-body contact, but each photo is a direct inspection and does not require route search or orientation-state planning. Both are credible L4 tasks with different bottlenecks; the courier is stronger on spatial route/control while Fluke is stronger on repeated visual identity bookkeeping.

evidence.explanation: The approved baseline is L4/full with an 18x11 course, five barriers, sparse scanners and 48-105 solution moves.
The generator solves a path constrained by open cells and orientation gates.
The grader replays each move and gate crossing and checks the completed route.
Fluke's dependent state is the identity/epoch sequence and exact required-set coverage, not a spatial route.

anchor_comparisons.concrete_comparison: The approved L5 candy task requires four valid adjacent swaps, and every accepted swap changes the board through multi-wave matches and refill while an exact score and forbidden licorice rule constrain the route. Fluke photos also advance to a new layout, but the animal's identity persists and there is no cascade, score search, inventory depletion or causal choice among future board options. Fluke L4 is therefore below this approved L5 planning/causal benchmark while still being harder than a one-shot visual selection task.

evidence.explanation: The approved baseline is L5/simplified with four changing-board swaps, at least seven waves and a five-item preview.
The generator enumerates valid routes over changing boards rather than merely repeating an independent action.
Success checks exact move count, exact score, cascade depth and no forbidden contact.
Fluke's shuffle changes positions and pose layouts but leaves the individual set and required IDs fixed.

visible_baseline_solution: At the L4/full baseline, a screenshot-only agent reads the two species named in the census list, moves the pointer over the 820x430 water canvas, and uses the orange lens plus the 280x220 inspection card to identify a body's species and tail-edge notch signature. It must remember which six individual IDs belong to the two listed species, keep the lens inside the exact moving polygon at shutter time, press Space, then repeat the inspection after each accepted photograph because the pod advances to a fresh shuffled layout and gives no persistent marks. It should avoid the three off-list individuals and previously photographed identities, then press Census complete after all six required individuals have been photographed once. A no-hit lens position is recoverable by repositioning; a duplicate or off-list hit closes the survey and requires a fresh attempt. The grader accepts only a monotone, mode-correct event transcript whose photos equal the required set and whose last event is submit.

baseline_judgment.rationale: Keep L4/full. The active configuration combines nine moving bodies, six required identities, three decoys, single-notch distinctions, full rotation and 20% scale variation, and a no-mark reshuffle after every accepted photograph. This is materially above the approved L2 one-click constellation and the approved L1 voxel mine on repeated 2D identity/memory decisions. It is below the approved L5 candy task's evolving-board causal search, while the approved L3 gyro and L4 dice tasks show that scalar levels compare different bottlenecks; Fluke's direct lens action is less physical than those tasks but its identity bookkeeping is substantial. The source supports the relative placement, but not an empirical human or agent calibration of an absolute L4 threshold.

evidence.explanation: The assigned baseline is explicitly difficulty 4 and full interaction.
L4's active parameters are nine animals, notch difference 8, rotation range 180 and scale range 0.2.
The generator creates three individuals per species, two listed species, separated moving layouts, pose variation and a required-ID set of six at L4.
The browser renders drifting poses, exact polygon inspection and the same animal's magnified tail card.
The authoritative replay ties each photo to the current moving layout and requires exact required-set coverage.

uncertainties: No human/VNC or computer-use-agent calibration was available or run; the absolute L1-L5 placement remains source-based.
The source proves tail geometry and hit-test consistency, but screenshot legibility and accidental-shutter rates across seeds still need the parent's runtime and visual checks.
No historical pre-controls generator/task snapshot is present, so historical preservation cannot be established from this source.
The browser receives the generated world as render state; this audit describes the normal screenshot-only path and does not treat private-state solver knowledge as task behavior.

profiles.visible_problem: Use Lens X/Y controls and Position lens to inspect a moving 2D body, then click Photograph for each of the two listed species. With one individual per species, identity bookkeeping is minimal; orientation and scale are stable, though position drift and post-photo reshuffling remain visible.
profiles.success_condition: The coordinate aim and photo_button sources must produce two distinct required individuals, with no off-list or duplicate photograph, followed by census_button submit; the grader requires exact required-set coverage.
profiles.rationale: This is the easy endpoint: two required individuals and one decoy, broad stable silhouettes, and no rotation/scale normalization. The persistent moving-lens and no-mark rules keep it from being a static selection task.

evidence.explanation: L1 parameters specify three animals, large notch separation and zero angle/scale range.
The generator makes one individual per species, lists two species and creates four layouts with motion metadata.
Simplified coordinate aiming and button photography use the same photo/reshuffle state machine.

profiles.visible_problem: Move the pointer over the 820x430 water canvas, use the lens/card to identify each of the two listed species, and press Space to photograph. The same moving, stable-orientation world as L1 simplified is used, with continuous pointer positioning as the input surface.
profiles.success_condition: Pointer aim and Space photo events must identify the two required individuals exactly once, followed by census_button submit; wrong-mode sources, duplicates and off-list photographs fail.
profiles.rationale: The world and decision problem are the L1 simplified profile; the full-mode difference is motor input, not an added puzzle rule. The broad stable shapes make this the lowest named profile.

evidence.explanation: The difficulty parameters are unchanged from L1 simplified.
Full mode binds pointer movement and Space while retaining the same photograph and submit logic.
The grader binds full mode to pointer/space and replays the same world hit test.

profiles.visible_problem: Use coordinate controls to inspect and photograph four required individuals among six stable-orientation bodies. Two individuals of each listed species now look alike except for their tail-edge notch pattern, so the agent must retain identity records across seven reshuffled layouts.
profiles.success_condition: Coordinate/photo_button events must cover all four required IDs once and only once, then census_button submit; the exact moving-polygon replay rejects stale identity or wrong source claims.
profiles.rationale: The count increase creates same-species identity ambiguity and a larger required set; this is a real decision/memory change, not credit for independent repetition alone. Orientation and scale remain forgiving.

evidence.explanation: L2 doubles the per-species identities and uses notch difference 18 while keeping pose variation at zero.
The number of individuals per species is n/3 and the tail notch carries individual identity.
The grader requires each required ID once and advances the layout epoch after each accepted photo.

profiles.visible_problem: Move the pointer and press Space to inspect and photograph four required identities among six stable-orientation bodies. The agent must use the card to distinguish two members of each listed species and remember prior photos after every reshuffle.
profiles.success_condition: Pointer/space events must cover all four required IDs once, then census_button submit; any duplicate, off-list or mismatched moving hit fails.
profiles.rationale: This has the L2 simplified world and state burden. Full pointer control changes how coordinates are supplied but does not add target count, visual variation, tolerance, or success requirements.

evidence.explanation: L2 active geometry is independent of interaction mode.
The card shows a magnified crop of the same focused animal and labels its species.
Full-mode source binding and replay use the same required identity and hit-test rules.

profiles.visible_problem: Use coordinate controls to identify four same-species pairs while their bodies appear at up to 65 degrees of rotation and 12% scale variation. Tail signatures are closer than L2, so the agent must normalize pose and scale from the magnified card before each of seven possible epochs.
profiles.success_condition: Coordinate/photo_button events must hit and claim each of the four required IDs exactly once at the current pose, followed by census_button submit.
profiles.rationale: The identity count is unchanged from L2, but the active rendered pose and tighter notch separation make visual matching under transformation harder. This is a perceptual increase, not a repetition quota.

evidence.explanation: L3 changes notch difference, rotation and scale while keeping six animals.
Each rendered layout carries angle and scale parameters that affect the generated pose.
The browser applies pose transforms to the body and to the inspection card.

profiles.visible_problem: Move a pointer lens over four required individuals whose tail signatures must be matched under 65-degree rotation and 12% scale variation; press Space after each inspection and retain the four-item census across reshuffles.
profiles.success_condition: Pointer/space events must claim the four required moving polygons exactly once and finish with census_button submit; the full transcript is checked against the same transformed world as simplified.
profiles.rationale: The full profile has the same active perceptual and memory demands as L3 simplified. Pointer motor positioning is the only interface change supported by the source.

evidence.explanation: L3's world parameters are mode-independent.
Full mode uses pointer and Space handlers but the same photograph state transition.
The grader changes only expected input sources by mode and otherwise replays identical world rules.

profiles.visible_problem: Use coordinate controls to identify six required individuals among nine moving look-alikes, distinguish single-notch identities with up to full rotation and 20% scale variation, and repeat the inspection after each accepted photo because all animals remain visually unmarked.
profiles.success_condition: Coordinate/photo_button events must hit all six required IDs exactly once in their current epochs and end with census_button submit; a duplicate or off-list photo terminates the attempt and the grader rejects incomplete coverage.
profiles.rationale: This is the assigned hard profile. It adds one same-species individual per listed species and one additional decoy relative to L3, tightens the notch difference, and activates the full pose range and 20% scale variation.

evidence.explanation: L4's parameters are nine animals, six required identities by construction, notch difference 8, full rotation and 20% scale range.
The visible list names two species while each focused body exposes its actual species and magnified tail.
The success replay requires exact six-ID coverage with no duplicate or off-list photo.

profiles.visible_problem: Move the pointer lens over nine moving bodies, use the magnified card to match six required identities despite full rotation and 20% scale variation, press Space for each, and remember the photographed set through ten shuffled layouts with no marks.
profiles.success_condition: Pointer/space events must hit the six required IDs exactly once at the correct epoch and finish with census_button submit; duplicate, off-list, stale or simplified-source events fail.
profiles.rationale: The full baseline is the same L4 decision, perception, memory and state transition as simplified. The direct pointer/Space surface adds motor precision but no separate target, physics or grading burden.

evidence.explanation: The assigned full baseline uses the L4 parameter set.
Full pointer/Space input feeds the common exact hit, photograph, epoch and submit logic.
Full mode is bound to pointer and space, while world replay and success are unchanged.

profiles.visible_problem: Use coordinate controls to inspect and identify eight required individuals among twelve look-alikes. Four members of each species, notch difference only 5, full rotation and 28% scale variation require fine tail comparison and a larger memory ledger across thirteen shuffled epochs.
profiles.success_condition: Coordinate/photo_button events must cover exactly the eight required IDs once, without any duplicate or off-list photo, and finish with census_button submit; the replay still requires a valid moving hit at every shutter.
profiles.rationale: The named top profile increases identity count and ambiguity while widening scale variation; rotation remains fully active. It is the hardest named Fluke profile, but not evidence that no harder world could exist.

evidence.explanation: L5 activates twelve animals, notch difference 5 and 28% scale range.
The generator makes four individuals per species and lists two of the three species, yielding eight required IDs.
Success remains exact required-set coverage, so the added burden is active visual identity and memory rather than a grader-only quota.

profiles.visible_problem: Move the pointer lens over twelve moving bodies and use the inspection card to match eight required tail identities under full rotation and 28% scale variation; press Space and remember the eight photographed identities through thirteen unmarked reshuffles.
profiles.success_condition: Pointer/space events must hit every one of the eight required IDs exactly once and end with census_button submit; the grader rejects duplicates, off-list photos and wrong interaction sources.
profiles.rationale: The full L5 profile preserves the same top-level visual and memory problem as simplified. The input surface is more direct, but no active world or success parameter differs.

evidence.explanation: L5 parameters and both implemented interaction surfaces are defined together.
Rendered pose and inspection geometry are common to both modes.
The only mode-dependent grader expectation is the input source map; the world, hit, epoch and success conditions are shared.

full.ordering_assessment: L2 is harder because same-species identity bookkeeping and the required set grow; the extra layouts are a consequence of the added state, not independent repetition credited by itself.

full.ordering_assessment: L3 is harder through active pose normalization and closer tail comparison, not through more actions or a grader quota.

simplified.ordering_assessment: L3 is a distinct perceptual profile: the card and body share transformed geometry, so matching cannot rely on a fixed orientation or size.

Pose transforms affect both the canvas body and its inspection card.

full.change: Animal count 6->9 raises required IDs 4->6, same-species members 2->3, distractors 2->3 and layouts 7->10; notch difference 12->8, rotation 65->180 and scale 0.12->0.20 also increase ambiguity and pose variation.
full.ordering_assessment: L4 is harder because both the identity ledger and transformed visual discrimination grow; the layout increase follows added individuals and changed epochs rather than acting as a standalone repetition bonus.

simplified.ordering_assessment: L4 remains ordered above L3 on the decision and perception burden; simplifying input does not remove the added target identities or pose changes.

evidence.explanation: The L3-to-L4 parameter changes are explicit and active.
The count controls per-species identity generation, listed required IDs and number of layouts.
The extra identities are part of authoritative success coverage, not merely UI display or minimum-action accounting.

full.change: Animal count 9->12 raises required IDs 6->8, same-species members 3->4, distractors 3->4 and layouts 10->13; notch difference 8->5 and scale 0.20->0.28 tighten identity matching and increase size variation while rotation stays at 180.
full.ordering_assessment: L5 is the harder named profile because the remembered set and near-lookalike count expand and the notch/scale variables remain active; this is a supported relative ordering, not an empirical claim about all possible L5 worlds.

simplified.ordering_assessment: The simplified L5 profile is ordered above L4 for the same active reasons; input abstraction does not erase the eight-item ledger or closer signatures.

The generator's n/3 construction yields four individuals per species and eight required IDs at L5.
Notch values directly change the rendered outline used for identity inspection.

baseline_preservation.current_default_equivalence: The explicit L4/full condition uses the same parameter values as the generator's BASELINE, and the assigned test asserts identical generated worlds at a fixed seed for the unconditioned task versus explicit L4/full. This establishes world equivalence for the tested comparison, not byte-identical challenge identity: the controlled condition is included in the challenge hash and public/truth identity.

evidence.explanation: The test explicitly grades both modes and rejects a full transcript against simplified truth/public state.
The two handlers feed the same photograph and submit functions, with mode-specific source labels.
The grader binds condition and event sources, then replays common world and success rules.

interaction_equivalence.world_information_goal_effects_success: Both modes share L5's twelve animals, eight required identities, four decoys, notch difference 5, full rotation, 28% scale variation, thirteen layouts and exact census goal.

evidence.explanation: The source tests cover both modes at all five levels and check world, determinism, hit invariants and mode-specific grading.
Both modes consume the same state animals/layouts and record the same event transcript structure.
Public-world equality, source binding, moving hit replay and exact required-set success are common to L5.

concise_summary: Keep Fluke Census at difficulty 4 with full interaction. Source evidence shows a real six-identity, moving, transformed-tail memory task with dependent reshuffles, a supported ordered ladder from L1 through L5, and mode-specific input binding that preserves the world and success rules.
limitations: This is source analysis only; no browser, VNC, multi-seed, exported-verifier or computer-use-agent check was run.
No human or agent calibration supports the absolute labels, so the level judgment is comparative and provisional.
Historical pre-controls preservation is unavailable; only current default versus explicit L4/full world equivalence is supported by the assigned test.
